title: Which Leatherman Should You Buy? Rev vs Wingman vs Wave+ vs Rebar vs Signal vs Surge
description: Leatherman makes a dozen look-alike multitools. Here is what actually separates the popular models, and which one fits the way you'll use it.
answer: For most people the Leatherman Wave+ is the one to buy: 18 tools, with the knives opening from outside so you don't unfold the handles. Pick the Wingman or Rev to spend less, the Skeletool CX to carry light, the Signal for camping, and the Surge for heavy daily work.

paras: Every full-size Leatherman has pliers, wire cutters, a knife and screwdrivers. What changes from model to model is how many extras you get, how heavy the tool is, and whether you can reach the blades without opening the handles.
Leatherman lists a 25-year warranty on all of the tools below, so the choice is about fit, not about which one will last.

The Wave+ has 18 tools in about 8.5 ounces, and its blades open from the outside with one hand, so you don't have to unfold the handles to cut something. That one detail is why it's the model people keep for decades. If you're buying one Leatherman as a gift and don't know much about the person's habits, buy this.

Both have 14 tools and both sit under $50 at Leatherman's own store. The Wingman's pliers and scissors are spring-loaded, so they open on their own, which makes it feel like a more expensive tool. The Rev skips the scissors and the springs. If you just want real pliers for the least money, get the Rev. If you'll use it every day, the Wingman is worth the small step up.

The Skeletool CX trims the list to 7 tools, the ones you actually reach for: pliers, wire cutters, a 154CM steel blade, a bit driver and a carabiner that doubles as a bottle opener. At about 5 ounces it's Leatherman's lightest pliers-based tool, and the easiest full-size one to forget you're carrying.

The Rebar is the plain workhorse of the lineup, with 17 tools, a saw and replaceable wire cutters. It doesn't have the outside-opening blades of the Wave+, so you open the handles to reach the knife. That's fine in a garage, less handy on a ladder.

The Signal is built for the outdoors. Among its 19 tools are a ferro rod for starting fires, a safety whistle, a hammer surface for tent stakes and a diamond-coated sharpener for touching up the blade. It's 4.5 inches long and about 7.5 ounces. Leatherman sells the sheath separately.

The Surge is the big one, with 21 tools and about 12.5 ounces. It has four locking tools that open from outside, spring-action scissors, a large bit driver and a holder that swaps between a saw and a file. It's too heavy for a pants pocket, so think belt, toolbox or truck door.

faq.q: What is the most popular Leatherman?
faq.a: The Wave+ is the model most people point to, because it balances tool count, size and outside-opening blades.

faq.q: Which Leatherman is best for everyday carry?
faq.a: The Skeletool CX if you want light and simple, or the Wave+ if you want more tools and don't mind a little more weight.

faq.q: What is the cheapest Leatherman worth buying?
faq.a: The Rev and the Wingman both have 14 tools and cost under $50 at Leatherman's store. The Wingman's spring-loaded pliers make it the nicer of the two.

faq.q: Do Leatherman tools come with a sheath?
faq.a: Not always. Leatherman's own pages list the sheath as sold separately for several models, including the Signal and the Rev, so check the listing before you buy.

title: Secret Santa Gifts Under $25 That People Actually Use
description: Office-safe gift exchange ideas under $25: small lights, good pens and pocket notebooks that won't end up in a drawer.
answer: The safest Secret Santa gifts under $25 are small things everyone uses: a keychain flashlight, an all-steel pen or a pocket notebook. None of them are blades, so they're fine for an office exchange.

sections.h2: Why small gear works for gift exchanges
paras: A gift exchange has two rules nobody writes down: stay under the limit, and don't give something the person has to find a use for. Small everyday tools pass both, because they solve problems people run into every week.
We left knives off this list on purpose. Plenty of offices don't allow them, and you rarely know the person well enough to guess.

A light on the keys is the gift people are surprised to use the most. It's there for the dark parking lot, the dropped earring and the porch lock, and it saves the phone battery. The Nitecore THUMB's head tilts, so it can hang off a bag strap and still point where you need it.

For the person who still writes things down. The Zebra F-701 is an all-steel pen that costs about as much as a coffee. Field Notes have a following of their own, so they read as thoughtful rather than cheap. Rite in the Rain is the pick for someone who works outside.
If the limit is tight, pair two small things. A Nite Ize S-Biner MicroLock with a Zebra pen, or a Rite in the Rain notebook with the pen, makes a neat little set for about the price of one gift.

faq.q: What is a good Secret Santa gift for a coworker?
faq.a: Something small and useful that isn't personal, like a keychain flashlight, a good pen or a pocket notebook.

faq.q: Is a pocket knife a good Secret Santa gift?
faq.a: Usually not for an office exchange. Many workplaces don't allow knives, so a light, pen or notebook is the safer pick.

faq.q: What can I get for $10?
faq.a: A Zebra F-701 pen, a Rite in the Rain pocket notebook or a pair of Nite Ize S-Biners all fit under $10.

title: Gifts for Hikers and Campers: Small Gear That Earns Its Spot
description: Useful gifts for people who spend weekends outside: a camping multitool, hands-free lights, a tough watch and gear that writes in the rain.
answer: Good gifts for hikers and campers are small, light and useful when things go wrong: the Leatherman Signal multitool, a light that clips on so both hands stay free, a G-Shock that shrugs off knocks, and a notebook that works in the rain.

paras: People who hike and camp count every ounce, so a gift has to replace something or solve a real problem. Big, single-use gadgets tend to stay home. Small tools that do several jobs go in the pack every time.

The Leatherman Signal is the standout. Along with pliers, a saw and a blade, it carries a ferro rod for starting fires, a safety whistle and a hammer surface for tent stakes. For a smaller budget, the Gerber Dime puts real pliers and a bottle opener on a keychain.

sections.h2: Lights that keep your hands free
paras: A light you have to hold is a light you put down in the dark. The Nitecore THUMB clips to a cap brim or pack strap and tilts to aim, and it has a red side light that's easier on night vision. The Olight Oclip Pro clips to a jacket or strap for dog walks and late arrivals at camp.

sections.h2: A watch that doesn't need babying
paras: The square G-Shock is built to take knocks and is water resistant to 200 meters. The solar GW-M5610U charges from light, so it never needs a battery swap on a long trip.

sections.h2: Write it down, even in the rain
paras: Trail notes, campsite numbers and the name of that bird all need somewhere to go. Rite in the Rain paper takes a wet day, and Fisher's pressurized cartridge is made to write in the cold and upside down.
For someone who already carries a knife, the SENCUT Sachse is a full-size folder that handles kindling, food prep and rope. Knife laws differ by state and park, so check before you gift a blade.

faq.q: What is a good gift for someone who loves hiking?
faq.a: Something light that does more than one job, such as an outdoor multitool, a clip-on light or a weatherproof notebook.

faq.q: Is the Leatherman Signal good for camping?
faq.a: Yes. It is Leatherman's outdoor model, with a ferro rod, a whistle, a saw and a hammer surface among its 19 tools.

faq.q: What is a good camping gift under $25?
faq.a: A clip-on keychain light like the Nitecore THUMB, or a Rite in the Rain notebook with a pen.

title: The Best EDC Flashlight for Your Pocket (Not Just Your Keys)
description: When a keychain light isn't enough: flat pocket lights, swivel-head lights and clip-on lights compared, from about $35 to a splurge.
answer: The best pocket EDC flashlight for most people is the Nitecore EDC09, because its head swivels and its magnetic tail lets it stand on its own while you work. Pick the Nitecore TIP3 to spend less, the Olight ArkPro Ultra or Nitecore EDC29 for a flat, phone-like light with more power, or the Olight Oclip Pro to clip on and keep your hands free.

paras: A keychain light is always with you but small. A pocket light is bigger, brighter and easier to grip, and it rides on a clip instead of your keys. If you already have a keychain light and keep wishing it were brighter, you're ready for a pocket light.

The EDC09 puts out up to 1,600 lumens, and its head swivels through 102 degrees. Add the magnetic tail and you can stick it to a car hood or stand it on a shelf and aim it into whatever you're fixing. It charges over USB-C.

sections.h2: Best on a budget: Nitecore TIP3
paras: The TIP3 is flat, clips to a pocket and reaches 720 lumens. It also lets you choose warm, neutral or cool white, which matters more than people expect: warm light is easier for reading labels and seeing true colors.

Flat EDC lights sit in a pocket like a phone instead of rolling around like a tube. The Olight ArkPro Ultra goes up to 1,700 lumens. The Nitecore EDC29 is the power pick, at up to 6,500 lumens, which is far more than daily chores need but very welcome on a dark road.
If you mostly need light while your hands are busy, a clip-on beats any pocket light. The Oclip Pro fastens to a pocket, a strap or a collar, which makes it a favorite for dog walks and runs.

sections.h2: How many lumens do you need?
paras: For finding keys, reading a menu or walking a path, a few hundred lumens is plenty. High output is for scanning a yard, a trailhead or the side of a road. Most good EDC lights let you start low and step up, so a high maximum doesn't hurt, but it shouldn't be the only thing you compare.

faq.q: What is the best EDC flashlight?
faq.a: For most people, a compact USB-C rechargeable light with a pocket clip and a range of brightness levels. The Nitecore EDC09 is our pick for its swivel head and magnetic tail.

faq.q: How many lumens should an EDC flashlight have?
faq.a: A few hundred lumens covers everyday tasks. More is useful outdoors or on the road, as long as the light also has low modes.

faq.q: Are flat flashlights better for pocket carry?
faq.a: Many people find them more comfortable, because they lie flat like a phone instead of rolling around in a pocket.

title: What Is EDC? A Plain-English Guide to Everyday Carry
description: EDC means everyday carry: the small, useful things you keep on you every day. Here is what goes in a basic kit and how to start without overspending.
answer: EDC stands for everyday carry: the small, useful things someone has on them every day, like keys, a wallet, a phone, a small light, a pen and a compact tool. A good EDC kit is light, legal where you live and made of things you actually use.

paras: Everyday carry is less a hobby than a habit. It is whatever you pocket on the way out the door so you are not stuck when a box needs opening, the power goes out or a form needs signing.
Most kits grow from the basics everyone already carries (keys, wallet and phone) by adding one or two small tools that solve problems you run into every week.

sections.h2: The five pieces most kits start with
paras: A small tool for cutting and fixing, a light that isn't your phone, a pen, something to write on and a way to keep your keys organized. You don't need all five on day one.
Start with one item that fixes a real annoyance. If you keep reaching for scissors, get a small multitool. If you keep using your phone as a flashlight, get a keychain light.

Add the next piece only when you notice you need it. A kit built that way stays light, because everything in it earns its spot. Our complete first kit under $100 is a shortcut if you'd rather start with a full set.

faq.q: What does EDC stand for?
faq.a: EDC stands for everyday carry, meaning the items a person carries with them every day.

faq.q: Is carrying a pocket knife legal?
faq.a: It depends on where you are. Knife laws differ by state and city, and some places limit blade length or opening mechanism. Check your local rules, or pick a tool such as a small multitool instead.

faq.q: What is the most useful EDC item?
faq.a: For most people it is a small light or a compact multitool, because both solve problems that come up every week.

title: How to Build an EDC Kit, Step by Step
description: A simple, budget-first way to build an everyday carry kit: pick a cutting tool, a light, something to write with and a way to organize your keys.
answer: Build an EDC kit by starting from what you already carry, then adding one item for each problem you hit often: a cutting tool, a light, a pen and a key organizer. Keep the whole kit light enough that you never leave it at home.

paras: Decide between a small multitool and a folding knife. A multitool is the safer bet for offices, travel days and anywhere knives draw looks. A folding knife cuts better and opens faster.
If you're not sure, start with a keychain-size tool like the Victorinox Classic SD or Gerber Dime.

sections.h2: Step 2: Add a light that isn't your phone
paras: A phone flashlight drains your battery and ties up your hand. A keychain light weighs almost nothing and is always on your keys.

sections.h2: Step 3: Carry something to write with
paras: A short pen and a pocket notebook cover the forms, phone numbers and lists your phone is slower for.
A small carabiner or clip keeps keys, a light and a mini tool together, and lets you split car keys off when you valet or lend the car.

sections.h2: Step 5: Carry it for a week, then adjust
paras: After a week, drop anything you never touched and upgrade the thing you used most. That is how a kit stays small and useful.

faq.q: How much does a basic EDC kit cost?
faq.a: A useful starter kit with a small tool, light, pen, notebook and key clip can come in under $100. See our first EDC kit under $100 for one example.

faq.q: Should my first EDC tool be a knife or a multitool?
faq.a: A small multitool is the easier first pick because it is welcome in more places. Choose a folding knife if you cut things often and your local laws allow it.

faq.q: Where do I carry EDC gear?
faq.a: Most people use a front pocket for a clipped knife or light, the key ring for small tools, and a back or chest pocket for a pen and notebook.

title: The Best EDC Knives Under $50
description: Real folding knives from Kershaw, Gerber, SENCUT, Buck and SOG that land under $50, sorted by size and style, with what each one is best for.
answer: For most people, the best EDC knife under $50 is a sub-3 inch folder from a known brand, such as the SENCUT ArcBlast or Kershaw Appa. Go bigger, like the SENCUT Sachse, only if you cut a lot outdoors.

paras: A blade under 3 inches handles boxes, tape, string and food prep without looking like a weapon. It is also the size most likely to be legal where you live.
If the knife will live in a dress pocket or go to someone who doesn't want anything tactical, pick a slim, classic shape.

sections.h2: Full size for outdoor and yard work
paras: A blade around 3 to 4 inches gives more reach for camping, gardening and breaking down a lot of cardboard.

Knife laws differ by state and city, and some limit blade length or how a knife opens. Check where you live, or where the person you're gifting it to lives, before you buy. Prices move often, so the buttons take you to today's price on Amazon or at the brand's own store.

faq.q: What blade length is best for EDC?
faq.a: Somewhere between 2.5 and 3.5 inches suits most everyday tasks. Under 3 inches is the most widely accepted size.

faq.q: Is D2 steel good for a pocket knife?
faq.a: D2 is a common tool steel on budget and mid-range folders. It holds an edge well, but it isn't fully stainless, so wipe it dry after use.

faq.q: Are knives under $50 worth it?
faq.a: Yes. Brands like Kershaw, Gerber, SENCUT and Buck make folders under $50 that people carry for years.

title: The Best Keychain Flashlights for EDC
description: Small rechargeable lights from Olight, Nitecore and Sofirn that live on your keys, plus when it's worth stepping up to a pocket light.
answer: The best keychain flashlight is one small enough that you forget it's on your keys until you need it. The Olight iMini 2 and Sofirn SE1 are easy starts under $25, and the Nitecore TINI 3 adds more output and a choice of light color.

paras: These are cheap enough to buy as stocking stuffers or to keep one on every key ring in the house.
Spending a bit more gets you more output, a choice of warm or cool light, or a clip so the light can ride on a pocket or strap.

sections.h2: When to step up to a pocket light
paras: If you walk the dog at night, work on cars or spend time outdoors, a larger pocket light gives far more reach. These ride in a pocket instead of on your keys.

faq.q: How many lumens do I need for an EDC flashlight?
faq.a: For finding keys, reading labels and walking to the car, a few hundred lumens is plenty. Higher output mainly helps outdoors and over distance.

faq.q: Are rechargeable keychain lights worth it?
faq.a: For most people, yes. USB-C charging means no spare batteries, and the light tops up with your phone cable.

faq.q: Is a keychain light better than a phone flashlight?
faq.a: It saves your phone battery, keeps your phone in your pocket and is usually brighter and easier to aim.

title: EDC Flashlight vs Headlamp: Which Should You Carry?
description: When a pocket flashlight beats a headlamp, when it doesn't, and why most people should carry a small flashlight every day and keep a headlamp in the car or pack.
answer: Carry a small flashlight every day, because it fits a pocket or key ring and is quick to aim. Keep a headlamp in the car, camping kit or junk drawer for jobs where you need both hands free for a long time.

paras: A flashlight is small, quick to grab and easy to point exactly where you need it: a keyhole, a dropped earbud, a fuse box. It also rides on your keys or clips to a pocket, so it's there when you didn't plan on needing light.

A headlamp frees both hands and points wherever you look, which is better for changing a tire, camping chores, long walks and repairs under a sink. The trade-off is bulk: few people want a headband in their pocket every day.

sections.h2: A middle ground: clip-on and magnetic lights
paras: Clip-on lights and lights with a magnetic tail cover a lot of headlamp jobs. Clip one to a collar or strap, or stick it to a car hood, and both hands stay free.

faq.q: Can a flashlight replace a headlamp?
faq.a: For quick jobs, yes. For long hands-free work like camping chores or car repairs, a headlamp or a clip-on or magnetic light is easier.

faq.q: What is the best light to keep in a car?
faq.a: A headlamp or a magnetic-tail flashlight, since roadside jobs usually need both hands.

faq.q: Do I need a tactical flashlight for EDC?
faq.a: No. A small rechargeable light with a few hundred lumens covers almost every everyday task.

title: Best Multitools for Everyday Carry, From Keychain to Full Size
description: How to choose between a keychain multitool, a pocket-size Leatherman and a full-size tool, with real picks from Victorinox, Gerber and Leatherman at every budget.
answer: Pick a multitool by size first. A keychain tool like the Victorinox Classic SD or Gerber Dime covers small daily jobs; a full-size tool like the Leatherman Wave+ is for people who fix things often and don't mind the weight.

paras: Tiny tools that live on your keys. They won't rebuild a bike, but they open packages, trim threads and tighten loose screws every week.
A step up with real pliers or drivers, still small enough for a front pocket.
Big, capable tools for garages, job sites, camping and the person everyone calls when something breaks. Expect more weight and a belt sheath.

faq.q: Is a multitool or a pocket knife better for EDC?
faq.a: A multitool is more versatile and more widely accepted. A pocket knife is better if most of what you do is cutting.

faq.q: Which Leatherman is best for everyday carry?
faq.a: For a front pocket, a smaller model like the Rev or Wingman. For people who use pliers daily, the Wave+ is the classic full-size choice.

faq.q: Can I fly with a multitool?
faq.a: Rules on blades and tools in carry-on bags vary by country and change over time. Check the current rules from your airport security agency before you fly, and pack it in checked bags if you are unsure.

title: The Best EDC Gifts for Dads
description: Practical everyday-carry gifts dads actually use, from a keychain light to a full-size Leatherman, sorted by budget.
answer: The best EDC gift for a dad is something he will use every week: a Leatherman multitool if he fixes things, a classic folding knife if he likes traditional gear, or a keychain light and a tough pen if you want to stay under $50.

paras: Small, useful gifts that don't need a big budget.
Bigger gifts that tend to get used for years.

Think about what he already does. A dad who fixes things wants pliers and drivers. A dad who walks the dog at night wants a light. A dad who still writes lists wants a pen that always works. Check local knife laws before gifting a blade.

faq.q: What is a good EDC gift for a dad who has everything?
faq.a: Upgrade something he already uses, like a better pocket light or a full-size multitool, rather than adding something new.

faq.q: Is a knife a good gift for a dad?
faq.a: It can be, if he likes knives and they are legal where he lives. A multitool is a safer choice if you're not sure.

faq.q: What EDC gift is best under $25?
faq.a: A keychain flashlight or a small keychain multitool. Our stocking stuffers under $25 guide has more.

title: The Best EDC Watches, From $25 to Splurge
description: Tough, simple watches for everyday carry: the Casio F-91W, the Casio Duro and the square G-Shock, and how to choose between digital, analog and solar.
answer: For most people the best EDC watch is a tough, simple Casio. The F-91W is the cheap classic, the Duro gives you an analog dive-watch look, and the square G-Shock is the one to buy if you want something built to take knocks.

paras: A light digital watch you can wear every day and not worry about. It's the default starter watch for a reason: it's cheap, simple and easy to replace.
If you want hands instead of a digital screen, a dive-style watch with real water resistance is the most practical everyday analog style.
The square G-Shock is shock resistant and water resistant to 200 meters. The solar, atomic-time version charges from light and sets its own time.

Digital is easiest to read and usually toughest. Analog looks better with a dress shirt. Solar costs more up front but saves you from regular battery swaps. Pick based on where the watch will be worn most.

faq.q: What is a good everyday watch for under $50?
faq.a: The Casio F-91W is the long-running budget pick. It's light, simple and inexpensive.

faq.q: Is a G-Shock worth it?
faq.a: If you work with your hands or play sports, yes. G-Shocks are built to be shock resistant and water resistant, so you don't have to baby them.

faq.q: What does Tough Solar mean?
faq.a: It's Casio's name for solar charging. The watch charges from light, so it doesn't need regular battery changes.
